claim: Windows SmartScreen judges a downloaded app on two signals: publisher reputation (signed + trusted cert) and file-hash reputation (clean download history).
quote: SmartScreen evaluates two signals when a user downloads and runs a file: 1. **Publisher reputation** — Is the file signed? Is the signing certificate from a known, trusted publisher? 2. **File hash reputation** — Has this specific file been downloaded by users without indications of malicious behavior?
location: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers
title: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers

claim: A signed but new binary (OV or EV cert) still shows a SmartScreen 'unrecognized' warning on early downloads; only unsigned apps get the stronger 'Windows protected your PC / Run anyway' block.
quote: | Valid Certificate (OV/EV) | ⚠️ Warning — app flagged as unrecognized until reputation accumulates; verified publisher name is displayed | | No signature | ⚠️ Warning — "Windows protected your PC"; User must choose "Run anyway" before the app can run. Enterprise policy can prevent continuation entirely. |
title: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers

claim: EV certificates no longer bypass SmartScreen reputation building — the instant-reputation behavior was removed; OV and EV now warn identically.
quote: EV certificates no longer bypass SmartScreen. Years ago, signing files with an Extended Validation (EV) code signing certificate would result in positive SmartScreen reputation by default, but this behavior no longer exists. ... Paying a premium for EV solely to avoid SmartScreen warnings is no longer justified.
title: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers

claim: SmartScreen reputation can take 'several weeks and hundreds of clean installs' to accumulate; unsigned releases restart from zero each version, while files signed with a consistent cert can inherit publisher reputation.
quote: There is no exact threshold, but it can take several weeks and hundreds of clean installs from a wide audience.
title: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers

claim: Windows 11 Smart App Control can block unsigned files entirely unless they already have positive reputation — stricter than SmartScreen prompts.
quote: On Windows 11 devices, the Smart App Control feature may supersede SmartScreen Application Reputation. Smart App Control will block execution of unsigned files unless the file has a positive reputation.
title: SmartScreen reputation for Windows app developers

claim: Microsoft's signing cost landscape (2026): Store MSIX = free signing by Microsoft; Azure Artifact Signing ~$9.99/month; OV cert $150-300/year; EV cert $400+/year.
quote: | **Microsoft Store (MSIX)** — Store re-signs your package | Free | ... | **Azure Artifact Signing** (formerly Trusted Signing) | ~$9.99/month | ... | **OV certificate** (from a CA such as DigiCert, Sectigo) | $150–300/year | ... | **EV certificate** | $400+/year |
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: Publishing as an MSIX through the Microsoft Store makes code signing free and automatic (Microsoft re-signs after certification); Store MSI/EXE submissions still require the publisher's own Authenticode cert chaining to a Trusted Root CA.
quote: If you publish your app as an **MSIX package** through the Microsoft Store, code signing is free and handled for you automatically — Microsoft re-signs the package after certification and you don't need to purchase or manage a certificate. If you publish as an **MSI/EXE installer** through the Store, you are responsible for Authenticode signing your installer before submission.
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: Azure Artifact Signing is geographically limited: organizations in US/Canada/EU/UK, individual developers only in US and Canada — an indie dev elsewhere must buy an OV cert.
quote: **Geographic limitation:** Azure Artifact Signing is available to organizations in the USA, Canada, the European Union, and the United Kingdom. Individual developers are currently limited to the USA and Canada.
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: Since June 2023 the CA/Browser Forum requires code-signing private keys (OV certs) to live on an HSM/hardware token — CAs ship a USB token or cloud-HSM option.
quote: **HSM requirement:** As of June 2023, the CA/Browser Forum requires private keys for OV certificates to be stored on a hardware security module (HSM) or hardware token. Most CAs provide a compatible USB token or cloud HSM option.
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: SignPath Foundation offers free OV-level code signing for qualifying open-source projects.
quote: If your project is open source, SignPath Foundation offers free code signing for qualifying open-source projects. The program provides OV-level certificate signing through a managed pipeline.
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: If an app registers a packaged MCP server for Windows agents, production releases must be signed with a Microsoft Trusted Root Program certificate — relevant because this dashboard ships an MCP server.
quote: If your app registers a packaged MCP server so that agents on Windows can use it, production releases must be signed with a certificate that is part of the Microsoft Trusted Root Program. A development certificate is fine for local testing.
title: Code signing options for Windows app developers

claim: winget publishing = a PR of YAML manifests to github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs; an automated pipeline validates policy/malware compliance, Microsoft can refuse any submission, and manifests may be manually reviewed.
quote: To submit your manifest, you'll upload it to the open source https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs repository on GitHub. After you submit a pull request to add a new manifest to the GitHub repository, an automated process will validate your manifest file and check to make sure the package complies with the Windows Package Manager polices and is not known to be malicious. ... Microsoft reserves the right to refuse a submission for any reason.
title: Submit your manifest to the repository

claim: winget acceptance criteria include: silent/non-interactive install, correct install+uninstall for admins and non-admins, virus-free, InstallerUrl served directly (HTTPS, no redirectors) from the publisher's release location.
quote: * The installer and application are virus free. ... * The application installs and uninstalls correctly for both administrators and non-administrators. * The installer supports non-interactive modes. ... * The installer comes directly from the publisher's website.
title: Submit your manifest to the repository

claim: Chocolatey community repo is human-moderated for every new package version (plus automated validator checking quality and verifier checking silent install/uninstall); 'trusted packages' from verified vendors skip human review.
quote: The community feed ... is a moderated feed. That means all new versions of packages are human reviewed prior to approval to check for safety, quality, and correctness. ... There are also trusted packages, which only go through automated moderation review and bypass human review as they are coming from trusted sources and/or the software vendors themselves.
title: Chocolatey Software Docs | Moderation

claim: Chocolatey requirements include ProjectUrl, licenseUrl, explicit 'trial/paid' mention in description, and proof of redistribution rights if binaries are bundled; packages unanswered for ~35 days are auto-rejected.
quote: ProjectUrl - it's required for the community feed ... If there is a license available, it **must** be included in the licenseUrl. ... The description should explicitly mention if this package installs trial software or software that needs a license present, or both.
title: Chocolatey Software Docs | Moderation

claim: Scoop distribution = JSON manifests in a git 'bucket'; official Main/Extras buckets exist, but anyone can publish an own bucket — BucketTemplate provides GitHub Actions that auto-update manifests every 4 hours.
quote: In Scoop, buckets are collections of apps. Or, to be more specific, a bucket is a Git repository containing JSON app manifests which describe how to install an app. ... Anyone can set up their own bucket with their own set of apps, and other people can add and install from this bucket—they just need to know the location of the bucket's Git repository.
location: What are buckets / Creating your own bucket
title: Buckets - Scoop Wiki

claim: WinSparkle is the Sparkle-equivalent for Windows: appcast (RSS) feed + single bundled DLL, native update UI, C API callable from other languages, silent unless an update exists.
quote: WinSparkle brings Sparkle-style software updates to Windows desktop applications. Publish an appcast, ship one DLL with your application, and let WinSparkle present a native update flow using your app's own name and icon.
title: WinSparkle

claim: Velopack is an actively maintained open-source (free) installer+auto-updater framework: background updates, delta packages, one-click per-user Setup.exe, portable self-update, code signing integrated, hosting on any static host incl. GitHub Releases.
quote: Background Updates — Perform updates in the background, launch the newest version on next launch. Small Delta Updates — Users only download the diff between versions ... One-Click Installer ... Self-Updating Portable ... Code Signing — Automatically sign and notarize (if applicable) your application during builds.
title: Velopack - A next-gen software installer and update framework

claim: Velopack is the de-facto successor to Squirrel.Windows (originated in the Clowd.Squirrel line); Squirrel.Windows itself is effectively superseded.
quote: I've been using Clowd.Squirrel since Squirrel.Windows wasn't working for me. Just popped into that repository and noticed the release of Velopack. How unexpected! It works fantastic and is so much faster than Squirrel, wow!
title: Velopack - A next-gen software installer and update framework

claim: For frozen Python apps the maintained update options (Nov 2026 check) are: Velopack (active, Python lib), tufup (quiet but not archived), hand-rolled version-check+installer; PyUpdater and Esky are archived, pywinsparkle dormant.
quote: | Velopack | Installer and updater with a Python library | 1.2.161, September 2026 | Active | | tufup | Updater built on The Update Framework | 0.10.0, October 2025 | Quiet for a year, not archived | | PyUpdater | Older updater for PyInstaller apps | 4.0, April 2021 | Archived | | Esky | Older freezer-agnostic updater | 0.9.9, September 2015 | Archived, unmaintained | | pywinsparkle | Python wrapper for WinSparkle | 1.6.0, April 2019 | Dormant, wraps WinSparkle 0.6.0 |
title: How to auto update a Python desktop app

claim: PyInstaller has no built-in update mechanism; with Velopack you must build --onedir (onefile is 'not compatible') and the vpk packaging CLI requires .NET SDK on the build machine only.
quote: Velopack's documentation is explicit about the first line: use `--onedir`, because the single executable from `--onefile` "is not compatible". The `vpk` tool needs the .NET SDK on your build machine. Your customers don't need .NET.
title: How to auto update a Python desktop app

claim: A Windows app cannot overwrite its own running files — the minimal self-update pattern is: check a version endpoint, download+verify the new installer by hash over HTTPS, launch it (e.g. Inno /SILENT /CLOSEAPPLICATIONS) as a separate process, and exit.
quote: Windows won't let you replace files that are in use. ... So the update has to be applied by something that isn't your app: a separate process, a script, or an installer that runs after your app exits. ... start the installer as a separate process and exit, so the installer can replace your files. The switches shown are Inno Setup's.
location: Why a Python app can't simply overwrite itself / Option 3
title: How to auto update a Python desktop app

claim: Self-rolled updaters must verify downloaded artifacts against a hash from the feed over HTTPS AND Authenticode-sign the installer, since a checksum alone doesn't satisfy Windows/SmartScreen.
quote: Verify what you downloaded against a hash from your feed, over HTTPS, before you run it ... Sign the installer. A checksum proves the download matches the feed. An Authenticode signature, added with SignTool, is what Windows and SmartScreen check
location: Three rules if you go this way
title: How to auto update a Python desktop app
